With grim irony I wonder if I wouldn't be better able to afford it if I didn't have taxes draining me dry to fund this sorry system which isn't sorry at all for me. I start to ask my family for help but stop short, instead I request my brother walk the dog for me and say no more. Something inside is resigned not to say more, I know they don't have much money either.

When the scheduler informed me that the earliest available appointment with a geneticist was in 14 months due to the shortage in fellowship training, I couldn't help but notice how my fingers felt stiffer than usual. "We used to train 20 fellows a year but after the NIH cut our T32 grant, we can only train 12 now," the scheduler explained, sounding apologetic as the words came through the receiver. "That means fewer specialists graduating, and our wait times have tripled," the scheduler continued, while I shifted the phone to my other hand, trying to find a comfortable position because the pain in my joints was getting worse. Hanging up the call, I begin to gather my thoughts, eyeing the various gig tasks I needed to tackle throughout the day. Each tap on the screen felt like a small jolt, my fingers struggling to cooperate as I tried to complete the list of tasks. I had to pause every few minutes, flexing my fingers and wincing slightly as I did so. Despite the awkwardness, I pushed through, clicking on another notification that came in. It was a struggle to focus on my usual cozy video games at night. The screen blurred as I tried to immerse myself, the pain a constant reminder that I needed to find a way to manage until my appointment. My partner sat beside me, watching a let's play on YouTube. The sound of the game was a little too loud, and each chime and beep seemed to echo in my head. I turned it down a notch, but it didn't help much. The background noise felt like a swarm of bees buzzing around. It felt like my usual Friday afternoons were slipping away because even the simplest things were becoming difficult to manage. I used to pick up the phone and call my favorite fast food place when I wanted a treat, but now the thought of holding the phone and navigating the app with my sore fingers felt almost unbearable. I just wish I could manage these small tasks without constantly stopping to rest my hands, but I am just trying to make it through each day the best I can. The pile of gig tasks doesn't get smaller, and my fingers don't get any better even though I keep hoping for some relief. I try to shake off the stiffness so that I can type out a message to the client waiting on an update, but each tap reminds me of how tight my fingers have become. I have to pause, take a deep breath, and begin again, slower this time. I watch as each letter appears on the screen, one by one, the backspace key becoming my companion as I struggle to correct the mistakes my stiff fingers make. The autocorrect seems to have a mind of its own, twisting my words into something unrecognizable. I squint at the screen, trying to make sense of the jumble before backspacing what I had typed, my fingers moving sluggishly, each keystroke a deliberate action as I attempt to formulate a coherent response. The room is dimly lit by a small lamp on the table beside me. The fluorescent light is not the best for these tiring eyes, but I squint harder, hoping it will help me focus just a bit more. My partner shifts next to me, glancing over with a concerned look but saying nothing. The silence is heavy, just like my hands that rest heavily on my lap, waiting for a break but knowing there will be no rest just yet. The workload demands my attention, and even though sitting here trying to shrug off the pain to get my tasks done, I know that I can't just let them pile up. It's like trying to climb a mountain while carrying a load of bricks, each step harder than the last. The phone feels like it weighs a ton in my hand as I scroll through the list of specialists, trying to find another geneticist with a shorter wait time, but it's a futile attempt. Each name blurs together as I try to decipher which one might offer a glimmer of hope or a quicker path to relief. But the search is overwhelming, and my fingers ache from just holding the phone. I put it down gently on the table and try to stretch my fingers, hoping to ease the stiffness that seems to settle in deeper with each passing day. The stretch offers a small moment of relief, but as soon as I let my fingers relax, the tightness creeps back in, wrapping around my joints like a vise. I glance at the clock, realizing it's already mid-afternoon, and I haven't even started my work for the day. The realization hits me, but I just pick up the controller, hoping a quick game will distract me from the relentless ache in my hands. I settle into the couch, the controller feeling awkward and cumbersome in my grip. The game loads up slowly, the bright colors flashing across the screen, but my eyes struggle to follow the movement. My fingers fumble with the buttons, and the character on screen stumbles awkwardly, mirroring my own struggle to maintain control. The game, once a refuge from my daily stress, now feels like an impossible challenge. This frustration is new, a kind of resistance I haven't felt before. My fingers, once nimble and swift, now struggle to keep up with even the simplest commands on the controller. It’s like they’ve taken on a mind of their own, refusing to cooperate with my intentions.

I find myself staring at the takeout menu more often, the idea of chopping vegetables or cooking meats just feels overwhelming. The kitchen stays quiet, filled only with pantry staples and the sound of paper rustling from takeout bags. I paused, and sighed loudly, not even attempting to hide my displeasure with her response, 14 months, pfft I could be DEAD by then! story_written: The room started getting dark and foggy. I didn't expect the gym to feel so surreal. The bass line from the track pushed another large, dark cube across the floor, steadily vibrating in place. Suddenly, darkness and a gray fog started coming into the room. I had never seen anything like it before. The snare hit and a muted red pyramid flickered rapidly, cutting through. Wow, I though to myself, this is unreal. I kept my eye on the slow drift of the deep, gray sphere released by the vocal note. It floated through the air while I tried to keep focus on the treadmill, while at the same time being transfixed by the way the shapes formed and dissolved around me. Each new sound added a different element to the room, a strange symphony of sights. I started wondering what would happen once the song ends? Does the color go back to normal, or is this a permanent change? I kept running, feeling the treadmill move beneath me, every step steady. A deep bass line dropped, and more colors emerged, dark hues spreading like ink across the horizon, one after another. A dark blue rectangle appeared on the ground, darker the faster I went and lighter in other times. So I slowed my pace to see how the rectangle would change. The hue softened a little, turning slightly lighter. The solid edges waved like gentle ripples in a pond. Hmm, I thought - my movement actually affects the shapes. I picked up the pace again, and the rectangle darkened once more, its shaped bluring the area.

I continue chopping vegetables, slowly and carefully, trying to minimize the jarring sensation in my jaw. When the receptionist answered, I explained my situation and asked for the earliest available appointment. The receptionist said the soonest they could see me was in two months. I asked why I wouldn't be able to get an appointment sooner, since I'm too young to be having these memory lapses. The scheduler explained, "We used to train 20 fellows a year, but now we only have sufficient funding to support 12 fellows." I told her, "I understand. Thank you for explaining." As I hung up the phone, I felt completely crestfallen. How could I ensure that I wasn't losing my mind? I use my brain for work, and with the memory lapses I was having, I could see it was failing me. I just wanted to feel normal again and to have my mind working as it used to, without the constant fog that seemed to permeate around me at all times.

This meant I had to devise a way to cope with the pain and increased difficulty I faced each day. Grading papers was a challenge, the pain in my hands increasing with every movement of the pen, and I was having much difficulty walking to the classrooms for my Friday meetings with students. The steps seemed steeper, and it became more difficulty to navigate the hallways without pausing to steady myself against the cool, brick walls. I also am having difficulties getting into my car, and with getting dressed in the mornings.  When I get home from work,  I feel exhausted from the effort of keeping up appearances, as if nothing is wrong.  I am so tired of my arthritis getting worse that I've started wearing slip-on shoes and clothes without buttons to make mornings easier. Now my employer is beginning to notice that I'm spending longer at my desk, avoiding trips across campus. They've asked if everything is okay, and my coworkers are wondering why I'm moving so slowly these days. I simply explain that I'm managing some health issues, brushing it off with a dismissive gesture.  It is not true however, and no one realizes how much time I spend recovering in bed from the severe pain and fatigue.  I don't know how I will keep managing like this while waiting for my rheumatologist appointment. Each day, the simple act of going to work and finishing my work day saps my energy. By the time lunch rolls around, I always take a moment to close my eyes and rest quietly at my desk before joining the others in the break room.  I just need a few moments to recover.  I will not be able to continue my Friday routine without some adjustments. I might have to try to find another doctor to work with.

I asked to schedule an appointment, so that I could be evaluated for possible early stages of Alzheimer's disease. The kind lady on the other end of the line explained, "I'm sorry, but the earliest available appointment we have will be in about 14 months from now.  We used to train 20 fellows,  but after the NIH cut our T32 grant, we can only train 12 now. That means fewer doctors are available to see patients, and our wait times have tripled," she said. I was in a bit of a shock. Feeling my symptoms were not getting any better, I really felt like I should be seen sooner. I went ahead and made the appointment, but decided to see if there were any other options. I spent the next few days calling other neurologists in Raleigh, only to hear similar stories about waitlists. I went ahead and put myself on each of the waitlists for a cancellation, just hoping something might open up sooner. As the weeks ticked by, I noticed small changes that were hard to ignore. Each Friday, I would head to the coffee shop with my book, but lately, I found it more difficult to get there, not because I forgot the way, but because I kept leaving my keys behind or misplacing my wallet. Once inside, I'd settle into a comfy corner chair, only to realize I'd forgotten my reading glasses again, which made the words in my book difficult to read and turned the anticipated pleasure of reading into a frustrating challenge. I rummaged through my bag, hoping I had brought them, but my search was not fruitful. I sat there squinting at the words, trying hard to make sense of the blurred letters. I strained, but it was futile to keep my focus as the letters swam on the page. Instead, I used my phone app to listen to the story instead while sipping my coffee. "Unfortunately, we're facing a severe shortage," the scheduler replied. "I'm worried my condition could get worse while waiting.” The scheduler continued, "We used to train 20 fellows a year, but after the NIH cut our T32 grant, we can only train 12 now. That means fewer specialists graduating, and our wait times have tripled." I thanked the scheduler and asked, "If there were any cancellations could I get on a waitlist?" I clutched the phone tightly. "Or are there any other facilities I should try so I can be seen more quickly?" She suggested checking other nearby facilities and added me to a waitlist for cancellations. I took the next available appointment and asked to be added to the wait list for any earlier openings. As I hung up the phone, my shoulders sagged slightly, and I looked around my cluttered desk. Papers were scattered everywhere, agenda notes mixed with student essays. I have too much work to be losing my memory, and I need to find a solution before things get even more hectic. As I think about making even more phone calls and jumping through more hurdles, I feel a sense of despair.

I thanked her for the information and proceeded to schedule an appointment for the next available date, even though it felt so far away. As the weeks passed, my vision seemed to get worse and worse. I found myself squinting at the labels on groceries when I stopped by the store on my way home from work. I noticed I needed to bring my phone closer to my eyes in order to read my friends' messages and I fumbled with the brightness settings to try to get my eyes to pick up on the screen's information. My guitar sheet music became harder to read and the notes blurred together as I tried to practice my favorite songs. I adjusted the lamp on my desk, trying to improve the conditions for my eyes as best I could, but I soon came to recognize the futility of all of this given that my eyes were simply not doing well by any stretch. I called the ophthalmologist again, wanting to see if I could be put on a cancellation waitlist. but they said they didn't have such a system in place at the moment. I hung up, feeling defeated and small.

There is a long pause on the other end of the line before the scheduler finally tells me, there is nothing they can do to get me in sooner. I ask if there are any other geneticists in the area who might have an earlier opening. The scheduler sighs and says, "I'm really sorry, but most places are experiencing the same issue. My hand shakes as I reach for the pen to jot down some notes, but the tremors make this task nearly impossible. The pen wobbles in my grip, and the letters come out jagged and unreadable. The receptionist informed me that the earliest I could see an oncologist was 14 months. This seemed crazy as we know with diagnosis and early treatment, outcomes are significantly better. When I asked the scheduler why the wait was so long, she explained that their hospital's fellowship program had lost government funding. They were operating with significantly fewer specialists and were overextending the number of patients they could see. After hearing the wait was 14 months, I immediately called my insurance to find another clinic. I decided to forego my Friday night work, even though with upcoming meidcal costs I would need the extra income. I was unable to find a clinic that could take me sooner despite calling every nearby facility listed by my insurance. I resigned myself to the long wait, knowing I'd have to keep pushing through. In the coming weeks, I pushed myself to keep up with my routine as best as I could. Every Friday, I would work at my practice and then go home to change into comfortable clothes and have a bit of dinner before getting on the road. The ongoing fatigue made the shopping trips for food delivery much more challenging and I had to opt out of those even though they had paid more than the average fast food delivery.

I explained that I needed to schedule an appointment with a psychiatrist, aware that managing my mental health is vital for keeping my life on track. The scheduler on the other end told me the earliest appointment available was 14 days from now. I said to the receptionist, "That is completely unacceptable. What do you mean 14 days? Can you get me something sooner?" The scheduler sighed and explained, "We used to train 20 fellows a year, but after the NIH reduced our funding, sadly, we have less than half that number. I know it's not an excuse, but I am telling the truth." I thought about this as I put the phone down, staring at it as I placed it on the kitchen table. I could feel my sanity slipping away and 14 days was much too long to wait. I told myself I will just have to find a way to manage until then.

story_written: Hello! I am calling about scheduling an appointment with a psychiatrist. I'm concerned about the wait time for getting help with my mental health. I was told that the wait could take up to 14 months, but I was wondering if there would be any way to reduce that? My mental health has been giving me a hard time lately, and the thought of waiting 14 months is hard to swallow. As the woman on the phone continued to explain, I have this wait due to the fact that they used to train 20 fellows a year, but after the NIH cut their T32 grant, they can only train 12 which is lengthening the wait time significantly. I hung up the phone and stared at my desk, the papers scattered. I begin to research other options for mental health support, but everything seems to have a long wait time just as the original clinic. I don't know how I will manage these long days at work, staring at the computer screen with my mind racing. Each Friday, I try and do my typical routine of unwinding, but the unresolved thoughts and racing mind make it hard to concentrate. I lower myself into the couch, holding a crossword puzzle shakily as I anticipate dissapointment from struggling to fill in even the simplest clues. The pen feels awkward in my hand, and my eyes are a bit blurry as I squint at the tiny squares in the puzzle. I sit and wonder how a psychiatrist could possibly help manage these thoughts cascading through my mind when the waiting period is so long and my symptoms keep getting worse. I try to focus on the crossword, but my hand trembles too much to write clearly. The letters look like a mess of scribbles, blending into each other. The letters on the crossword remind me of my current state, where everything feels disorganized and out of control. I set the crossword aside and glance at the clock; imagining the 14 months passing me by and wondering how I will cope in the meantime. I decide to try some light exercise, hoping it might help.

I asked what to do if the swelling gets worse, and she said I should try to manage it at home as best as I can, elevating my legs and using ice packs when needed," she added, sounding sympathetic but resigned. I hung up the phone, noting the time. A couple of days later, I headed to the softball field with my team, but the usual excitement I felt was overshadowed by the heaviness in my legs and lack of energy. I thanked him, slipping them on and adjusting the straps, feeling the compression offer some relief.

story_written: I found the number to make that call I needed to make to schedule an appointment at the oncologist because it's time for my post-mastectomy checkup.  I hope they have an appointment time that fits into my schedule soon, but when I spoke with the scheduler, she let me know the next available appointment was 14 months away. I was stunned to learn this! I've never had to wait more than a year before! "What did you say, 14 months? That's over a year!" I said, gripping the phone tighter. The scheduler explained, "We used to train more fellows, about 20 each year, but after the NIH cut our numbers have dropped to 12. That means fewer specialists graduating, and our wait times have tripled." As I set the phone down, I looked at the dishwasher, but didn't really see it as I thought about how long 14 months really is. I noticed the faint hum of the dishwasher filling the kitchen, but my thoughts were on all the days ahead before I could see the oncologist. I could hardly imagine how I would manage with this fatigue for over a year. Bringing in the recycle bin, I paused halfway down the driveway, my arms feeling as heavy as if I'd been carrying two bins at once. There has to be a way to make this work, I thought as I looked at the recycle bin sitting by the roadside. What if there is a cancellation? and they call me to come in sooner? It wouldn't hurt to check...  I called back to ask if I could be put on a cancellation list. The receptionist said, " "The cancellation list has been set up, and we'll reach out to you as soon as something opens up,” the receptionist said. I resolved to call every week until I got an update or an earlier appointment, if possible. As I finished up my usual Friday routine, I felt the familiar ache in my joints make itself known more prominently than before. My fingers stiffened slightly when I reached for the vacuum robot, not really paying attention to what I was doing and accidentally switched it to a different cycle I hadn't intended.  I can't go on like this so I decided to break tasks into smaller steps. After finally getting the recycle bin inside, I sank into my chair and let out a long breath, feeling the relief of resting my heavy arms and body against the cushion. I reached for the remote, flicking on the Roku TV to look at my usual YouTube favorite channels to get my mind off the discomfort in my joints. As the videos played, I found it hard to focus, the pain in my body seemed to seep into my concentration, pulling my attention away from the screen.

story_written: I picked up my cell phone and dialed the number. asked for an appointment with a psychiatrist and listened as the scheduler explained that the soonest available slot was 14 months away. "Sorry, ma'am. We are having fewer specialists because we used to train 20 fellows a year, but after the NIH cut our funding we can only train 12 now. That means fewer specialists graduating, and our wait times have tripled," she said. I hung up feeling defeated. What was I going to do now? I set my phone down on the kitchen counter and looked around the room. The dishes from breakfast were still piled up in the sink, my son was waiting on me to answer his questions from schoolwork. I wanted to cry. I sat down at the kitchen table, trying to focus on my son's math problems. His voice seemed distant as I tried figure out what he was asking about fractions. The table felt hard and uncomfortable against my elbows as I leaned in and tried my best to focus. That afternoon, I moved to the living room to scroll through videos on social media, hoping to find some relief from the cluttered kitchen and the growing sink of dishes. My husband came in and asked me what was wrong. I looked up from my phone, the screen glowing from my doom scrolling through endless videos. "Just trying to take a break," I mumbled, not meeting his eyes. The living room felt more cramped than ever before. I picked up my phone and water and went to my bedroom to escape the mess for a moment. The moment I stepped into the bedroom, I noticed the laundry basket overflowing with clothes in the corner. I sighed, "When will life stop feeling like it's piling up around me?" I placed the phone and my water on the dresser, rubbing my temple. My head was exploding from the stress. I prayed. "God give me strength to get through this wait," I whispered, feeling the coolness of the dresser on the palm of my hands. I then felt an overwhelming ease wash over me as I sat down on the bed and took a deep breath, letting the air fill my lungs slowly. The quiet of my room filled the air. I felt like everything would be ok, manageable, even if just for a moment. But then I remembered the psychiatrist appointment was still 14 months away, and the feeling of ease slipped away. As I sat on the bed, the feeling of stressed weighed me down and I knew I had to figure something out.

I cannot wait a whole year and two months to have my condition looked at. It could get way worse in that time. I tried to focus on my work all evening, but the pain in my joints made it difficult to type responses for the surveys. I had the pain in my hands kept getting in the way. Each keystroke felt like tiny needles stabbing me. I quit that and ate a snack instead. before deciding to try playing some video games to unwind. I sat on the couch, controller in hand, but my fingers felt stiff and awkward. I sobbed quietly into the sleeve of my sweater, hoping the sound wouldn't carry through the thin walls of my apartment. I put the controller down. I called some more offices, hoping another clinic might have an earlier opening. My phone felt heavy in my hand as I scrolled through the available doctors. I comared them to what my insurance could cover. Insurance was always a challenge, with its endless terms and conditions. I selected an office and called. I waited as the phone rang, tapping my fingers on the table. The receptionist answered, and I quickly explained my situation, wondering if I would have better luck this time. She said they could only offer an appointment in 16 months. That was even worse. I called another doctor. That one said they couldn't see me for 18 months. I sighed heavily, feeling the weight of my phone in my hand. What the heck. This was so dumb. I looked at the Internet for more information. It said that rheumatologists are in high demand due to a shortage, which was caused in part by cuts to training. This is dumb. Someone has to go donate some money to medical training. I brainstormed ways to raise awareness for this issue.

"Our fellowship cuts now have a 14-month backlog," she pauses before explaining, "We used to train 20 fellows a year, but now we can only train 12. The first one I called had a voicemail message, so I left my name and number. The next therapist had the same backlog, and I hung up the phone, feeling the weight of another long wait. story_written: My osteoarthritis is unbearably painful right now and I really need to get some sort of treatment. I need to call to schedule an appointment with a rheumatologist even though I learned it'll be a 14-month wait period because the scheduler explained that their hospital's fellowship training program just lost. I wonder if I should look into other options while I wait for the rheumatologist appointment. As I hang up the phone, I get online to research other clinics in the area, perhaps smaller ones that might have an opening within the next days or weeks. After a while, I find a few options that seem promising. I jot down their contact information and decide to give them a call right after my walk. It's Friday afternoon, and though my joints are stiff, I don't want to miss my usual walk. I put on my walking shoes, but the laces take longer to tie today. I head outside, holding my phone, but making sure to wrap the lanyard around my wrist because my fingers feel clumsy, and I'm afraid it might slip from my grip. The familiar path feels longer as I trudge up the inclines and  step carefully on the uneven ground, mindful of my knees protesting with each step. The podcast in my ear is a welcome distraction, and I'm thankful to have it playing as I slowly make my way back home, though I notice it’s harder to be motivated to complete the entire loop lately. Each step requires more effort, and I pause more often, adjusting my stride to ease the dull throb in my knees. When I finally arrive back home, I decide to cut my walk short for the next couple of weeks, hoping that with some rest, the pain might not be so pronounced. My neck feels stiff as I change out of my walking clothes and I have a cervicogenic headache that lingers as I settle into the chair at my desk. I think I need treatment of some sort because the stiffness in my joints is making it hard even to hold a pen. I try typing instead, but my fingers feel sluggish, and my handwriting has become almost illegible over time. I feel like a muscle relaxant  would help, but the thought of relying on medication long-term doesn't sit well with me. So, I decide to try some gentle stretches instead, hoping they take some pressure of the affected areas. As I slowly raise my arms above my head and bend my neck, I feel a little relief in the tension, but it's fleeting. The stiffness returns as soon as I relax my arms. I move to the kitchen, where I pour myself a chamomile tea, hoping the warmth will soothe my aching joints.  I wonder of the gentle heat from the tea will ease the stiffness in my fingers enough to hold a book later. I wonder what is the answer to the shortage of rheumatologists, and if the NIH will ever restore their grant program. I hope I can find other ways to manage until my appointment. I go outside with my Kindle  and settle into the sunniest spot I can find, propping it up on a small table to relieve my fingers of having to hold the device. Will physical therapy help? I've read that it can offer relief for people in my situation. Still, I wish there was a magic solution that could ease the soreness permanently, but I know that isn't real. Instead, I adjust the cushion behind my back and close my eyes, enjoying the warmth of the sun on my face, trying to relax amidst the growing noise of distant lawnmowers and chirping birds. The warmth spreads across my skin, and I listen carefully for some auditory therapy as the birds chirp and the trees rustle. Sometimes I think  about how different life was before the arthritis became this pronounced, how I would effortlessly hold a book for hours or type without thinking twice. I remember that my grandmother suffered from arthritis as well, and her knuckles always looked swollen and a bit twisted. She used to tell me how she needed to massage her hands every morning just to get them moving again. I do remember her doing that. When I look at my swollen fingers, what I see are her fingers now. I wish  there was  a way to reach the rheumatologist sooner. As I gingerly flex my hands, I grab some Myoflex cream from the side table and gently rub it into my knuckles, hoping it will ease the swelling a little. Perhaps another type cream might provide more relief, so I make a note to research some alternatives later. With a sigh, I try to relax. I think distraction is the key for now, so I press the button on my smartwatch and say, "play new episode of My latest podcast," letting the familiar voices fill the air around me. It's something I can still enjoy without needing to think about gripping anything tightly, just letting the sound wash over me as I sit there, trying to focus on the stories and insights rather than the stiff joints that refuse to bend easily like they used to. With each new episode, I let the dialogue take me away.  I will call to check if there are any cancellations or openings that might allow me to see the specialist sooner, but until then, I rely on my distraction methods to keep daily life manageable. My friends  also suffer from various ailments, and we often find ourselves comparing notes on the best physicians and various treatments that help us get through the day. We laugh together over our collective struggle with technology, as our hands aren't quite what they were just a few years ago . The buttons on our phones seem to shrink as our fingers get  stiffer. Tapping out even a simple message takes longer b ecause my fingers don't move as quickly or smoothly. I find that I am falling  more often, too as my balance seems to be affected by the stiffness in my knees and hips and feet. So, it's dangerous to walk too far from the house alone. I always make sure to carry my phone in my pocket when I venture outside or to a store because if I need help, I can call someone with just a touch. Could shoes with more support make a difference? I decide to research that, because the right pair might provide some stability and ease the strain on my knees and hips, potentially preventing any more falls. I hope that with a little more support, I'll be able to go places without worrying about stumbling.

story_written: I dialed the number and waited as it rang. I was hoping to schedule an appointment with a pulmonologist, but when the secretary answered the phone and informed me that the next available appointment was 14 months away, my mind went blank for a moment. The secretary explained, "I'm so sorry. We are booking out quite a way at this point because of the recent changes in our training program. We used to train 20 fellows a year, but after the changes in our NIH T32 grant, we can only train 12 now. That means fewer specialists are available to address the growing demand, so our wait times have tripled." I thanked the secretary and hung up, sitting back in my chair and wondering how I was going to manage the next year with my symptoms getting worse. As I returned to my computer, I noticed the wheezing getting even worse than it was before, and I started to get anxious. because I had a Zoom call scheduled in a few minutes. I needed to be completely on my game and available for the call, but the wheezing made it hard to concentrate on what I needed to say or do. As the meeting began, I tried my best to keep things together, but my focus kept slipping as the sound of my own labored breathing filled the room. I muted my mic and took a moment to collect myself. I wasn't sure how much longer I could keep this up. After the call ended, I decided to stretch my legs and take a break. I walked around the block after letting my boss know I needed some fresh air. The usual crispness of the breeze felt different this time as I wheezed more than usual, each breath feeling like a small challenge. I wondered if I would be able to finish the afternoon's tasks at my regular pace, knowing that I wasn't feeling as sharp as I needed to be. Returning to my desk, I found myself hesitating before sitting back down. The stack of IT tickets seemed to loom over my desk, more overwhelming today than usual. I rubbed my chest subtly, hoping to ease the tension and anxiety as I opened the first ticket. The words on the screen seemed to jumble together, and I had to squint and focus harder than usual. I really needed to take more frequent breaks to gather myself. The wheezing wasn't letting up, and I wondered if I needed medical attention now. I wasn't sure how I would manage the rest of the day at this pace, or what would happen if I needed to step away more often. I glanced at the clock, calculating how much time I had left before the end of the day, and it seemed like an eternity. Each minute felt longer than the last. Was this an issue with all of the clinics in the area, or was it just this one? I picked up the phone and started calling around to see if anyone else could offer an earlier appointment with a pulmonologist. When I called the second clinic, the receptionist informed me that they were experiencing the same delays. "I'm sorry, but we just don't have enough pulmonologists available right now," the receptionist explained. "We used to have so much availability, but things changed after the NIH cut our T32 grant. We can't get you in until then either, and the earliest appointment we can manage is 14 months from now." I hung up and took a break. Did I need to seek emergency care, or would I manage until I could see a specialist? The indecision weighed on me as I wondered if my health or my financial situation would win out in the end. I decided to try and manage for now, taking slow, deliberate breaths as I returned to my desk.

story_written: i start to make a call to the opthalmologist. i dial the number and wait for someone to pick up. When the scheduler answers, i begin to speak and explain that I need to make an appointment because my vision has been getting worse. The scheduler tells me to hold on for a moment while they check the schedule. The line is quiet, except for the occasional rustle of papers. After a minute, he comes back on the line and explains, "I'm sorry, sir , but the earliest available appointment we have is 14 months away. Our fellowship training program lost its NIH T32 training grant, and we have reduced our fellow intake from 20 fellows a year down to just 12," he explains. i freeze as I hear the number "14 months," my hand still resting on the edge of the kitchen table. The scheduler's voice continues, as you know, this cut means fewer specialists are graduating, and our wait times have tripled." I do not understand how I am going to manage until then." what should I do if I can't manage simple tasks anymore? I put the phone down and rest my head in my hands, feeling the weight of it crash onto my shoulders, before I slowly make my way to the living room. i think about how just last week, I was standing at the sink, washing dishes. The water was running, and I accidentally poured dish soap directly into the rinsing water instead of onto the sponge. It took me a minute to see what I'd done as the bubbles filled the sink oddly in a place that it shouldn't have. I fumbled, trying to scoop the bubbles out with my hands, watching the soapy water overflow onto the counter. My hands slipped, and the sponge fell into the sink, getting lost in the mess. I reached blindly, at the remote control on the coffee table, knocking over the pile of unopened bills that had been waiting for me. They scattered across the floor, some disappearing beneath the couch. My attempts to pick a bill from the floor resulted in me bumping my head on the edge of the coffee table. I winced and sat back on the sofa, rubbing the sore spot on my leg and stared blankly at the television screen, the picture just a blur of colors. I reach for the glasses that usually help me, but it's getting harder to find them amongst the clutter on the table. Once I manage to put them on, i can barely make out the figures on the screen. The TV show I've watched for years now seems like distant shapes moving around, and I can't follow the story like I used to. I squint and lean forward, trying to focus, but it doesn't make much difference. The details are all fuzzy, distorted and I struggle to piece together what's happening in the show. With the sound turned up to make up for what I can't see, the dialogue becomes a blurb of noise that fills the room, but doesn't really connect. I stretch my legs out on the couch, feeling the strain from bending my back at an awkward angle to fetch a missed bill hidden far under the couch. The day's small mishaps accumulate in my muscles as an unspoken reminder that I need to see the ophthalmologist. But the thought of waiting 14 months for an appointment gnaws at me. I shuffle to my side table, my fingers brushing against the worn-out wood, searching for the list of things I had planned to do that day.
